mcqs.question: Why can two consecutive reads of the same /proc file return different content?
options: /proc files are cached for a few seconds and occasionally refresh mid-read
/proc is a pseudo-filesystem — the kernel generates each file's content fresh at read time from live state, rather than reading stored bytes
/proc content only changes when the system is rebooted
This only happens if you have root privileges
mcqs.explanation: Because /proc files aren't backed by disk storage, the kernel computes their content at the moment of the read — so two reads a moment apart can legitimately differ if system state changed. There's no caching layer causing this, no reboot requirement, and privilege level doesn't affect it.

mcqs.question: In /proc/[pid]/status, what does a State value of 'D' indicate, and why does it matter operationally?
options: The process has exited but not been reaped — matters because it wastes a process table entry
The process is uninterruptible sleep, usually blocked on I/O — matters because it can't even be killed with SIGKILL while in this state
The process is stopped by a debugger — matters because it will never resume on its own
The process is running normally — matters only for CPU accounting
mcqs.explanation: 'D' means uninterruptible sleep, typically waiting on I/O like a slow disk or an unresponsive NFS mount — and while in that state, even SIGKILL can't remove it until the I/O completes or times out, which is a common cause of processes that 'won't die.' A defunct-but-unreaped process shows as 'Z' (zombie), not 'D'.

mcqs.question: How does `top` get the CPU and memory numbers it displays for every process?
options: It has a privileged kernel API unavailable to normal user processes
It repeatedly reads the same /proc files any user process could read, like status and stat under each /proc/[pid]/
It queries a separate system daemon that tracks process statistics
It computes the numbers itself by sampling CPU registers directly
mcqs.explanation: top has no special access beyond normal file permissions — it polls the same /proc/[pid]/ files any process could open and read, then formats and refreshes the view. There's no privileged API, no separate stats daemon, and no direct register sampling involved.

mcqs.question: In /proc/[pid]/maps, a memory region shows permissions 'rwxp' with no backing file. Why might a security reviewer flag this?
options: It means the process has crashed and this is leftover core-dump memory
A region that is both writable and executable, with no file backing it, is a common shape for injected or self-modifying code — legitimate code rarely needs both at once
It indicates the process is using more memory than its cgroup limit allows
'rwxp' always means the region belongs to a shared library
mcqs.explanation: Writable-and-executable anonymous memory is unusual for normal code (which is typically read-execute for code, read-write for data, kept separate) and is a pattern associated with runtime code generation or injected payloads. It doesn't indicate a crash, a cgroup limit breach, or shared-library status specifically.

mcqs.question: A monitoring agent polls /proc/[pid]/smaps for every process on the box once per second and the box's CPU usage spikes. What's the most likely cause?
options: smaps is cached, so this workload should be free — the spike must be unrelated
The kernel must compute detailed per-mapping memory data on every read, and doing this for every process every second adds real, measurable CPU cost
/proc reads always cost the same regardless of which file is read
smaps can only be read once per process lifetime, so the agent is erroring out and retrying
mcqs.explanation: smaps is one of the more expensive /proc files to generate — the kernel walks detailed per-mapping statistics on every read — so polling it for every process at high frequency is genuine, avoidable kernel CPU load, not a caching illusion. It has no per-process read limit and different /proc files vary widely in cost.

mcqs.question: Why is reading /proc generally preferred over attaching a debugger when investigating a suspected file-descriptor leak in a live production process?
options: Debuggers cannot read file descriptor information at all
/proc reads add negligible overhead and don't pause or alter the process's timing, unlike attaching a debugger which can mask timing-sensitive bugs
Attaching a debugger to a production process is against POSIX standards
/proc data is more accurate than what a debugger would report
mcqs.explanation: The key advantage is the lack of observer effect — a simple file read doesn't pause the process or change its scheduling, while attaching a debugger can alter timing enough to hide a race condition. Debuggers can read fd info, there's no POSIX prohibition on attaching in production, and accuracy isn't the differentiator here.
